case_study_insert.main_stem: Sorrel Bay Apart-Hotels (SBA) is a public limited company in the hospitality and apart-hotel sector, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 2004 by Farah Qureshi, the group operates serviced apartments around the Sorrel Bay marina and uses a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. SBA plans to invest $2,400,000 in 30 new serviced apartments at the marina, financed by a $1,500,000 share issue and $900,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $480,000 a year, a variable cost of $28 a unit and a selling price of $52, and currently produces 38,000 units a year. SBA faces two operational problems: labour turnover among housekeeping staff has reached 22% and guest complaints about maintenance delays have risen.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — Q3 2026: The 148 serviced apartments recorded 33,200 guest-nights last quarter, up from 29,400 a year ago, at an average occupancy of 78%. Maintenance requests averaged 140 per month with an average resolution time of 2.6 days, down from 3.4 days a year ago. Guest complaints fell from 64 to 41 per month. A survey of 750 guests found 66% prefer contactless check-in and 57% rate housekeeping consistency their top priority. A skills audit found 26 of 120 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the contactless check-in system; off-the-job training at the maritime college costs $750 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Sorrel Bay Apart-Hotels as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing borrowing costs for variable-rate finance. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $12.10 to $12.85 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills across the hospitality sector. (3) Domestic tourism spending grew 5.6% year-on-year, building-material costs rose 8.3% and services inflation stands at 6.4%, while short-stay regulation has tightened in the marina district.

questions.question_text: SBA plans to finance part of the marina apartments with a $1,500,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for SBA of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the share issue.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit carries no obligation to pay dividends on new shares, so the $900,000 stays inside the business to fund the build and to protect SBA's cash position as building-material costs rise 8.3%. Unlike a share issue, it does not dilute existing shareholders or create market pressure to maintain payouts, which matters for a public limited company answerable to investors who will scrutinise every $2,400,000 the marina build consumes.

Point 2: Retained profit involves no issue costs, no underwriting fees and no roadshow marketing, and it is deployed immediately without waiting for shareholder approval or subscription. SBA can lock in the 30-apartment construction slot before material costs climb further, keeps Farah Qureshi's control undiluted, and signals financial strength to the market without the discount often applied to new share issues, protecting the $52 average rate economics across the 38,000 units sold this year and reassuring the 750-strong guest base that SBA is building from profit, not from fragile balance-sheet stretch.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development applied to SBA's financing decision and market.

questions.question_text: SBA is launching its 30 new marina apartments. Consider a national television campaign, travel-agency partnerships, or social media influencer marketing with travel creators. Which should SBA choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television campaign: TV would reach millions and build rapid awareness of Sorrel Bay Apart-Hotels nationwide, suiting a public limited company with national distribution ambitions. However, primetime costs are prohibitive against an $2,400,000 expansion already funded through a share issue, much of the audience has no travel intent for the Sorrel Bay marina, and the message cannot be tailored to the 66% of guests wanting contactless check-in or the 57% who prioritise housekeeping consistency.

Travel-agency partnerships: Agencies can place apartments with business-travel and relocation clients, feeding a pipeline for the 33,200 guest-nights recorded last quarter; they reach planners immediately but charge commission, weaken the direct guest relationship and reduce control over the $52 rack rate — particularly for a new-build property without an agency track record.

Social media influencer marketing: Travel creators specialising in marina and apartment content reach exactly the domestic-tourism audience driving the 5.6% spending growth; short-form walkthroughs can show contactless check-in, marina views and housekeeping standards, with bookings measurable from click to check-in. Cost per influenced booking is low, and SBA keeps direct guest relationships and full margin.

Recommendation: SBA should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the fast-growing domestic segment at a fraction of TV's cost, preserves the $52 rate better than commission-based agencies, and showcases differentiators that 66% and 57% of guests already demand. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a marina-specific launch; travel agencies are rejected as margin-diluting and control-reducing, though SBA should retain a small agency presence for corporate relocation clients as a secondary channel.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of SBA with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of SBA with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and travel-agency partnerships are rejected.

questions.question_text: SBA's labour turnover among housekeeping staff has reached 22%. Explain two benefits for SBA of using democratic leadership to improve motivation in its housekeeping team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives housekeeping staff a genuine voice in scheduling, room-assignment systems and the contactless check-in rollout, meeting social and esteem needs (Maslow) and raising commitment. Staff consulted on how 148 apartments are turned between 33,200 guest-nights feel valued, directly reducing the 22% turnover and the disruption to occupancy running at 78%.

Point 2: Involving staff surfaces practical ideas — which maintenance issues to flag at check-in, which cleaning sequences cut the 2.6-day resolution time further — improving the housekeeping consistency 57% of guests rate their top priority. Lower turnover saves recruitment, referencing and retraining costs across a workforce of 120, protects the employer brand ahead of the marina expansion, and supports the democratic culture needed to absorb the April 2026 rise to $12.85 per hour without disputes or poor morale. Herzberg's motivators — achievement, responsibility and recognition — all strengthen when housekeeping teams help design the room-turn standard rather than simply being told it.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to SBA's turnover, occupancy and contactless rollout.

questions.question_text: SBA must train 26 staff on the new contactless check-in system. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the maritime college. Which should SBA choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Learning the contactless check-in workflows live on shift keeps all 26 staff productive, matches the exact marina property setup and costs nothing in fees; supervisors can coach at the front desk during real arrivals, reinforcing the 66% guest preference for seamless check-in. Drawbacks: mistakes affect real guests at peak times, trainers lose their own productivity, and no formal certificate is issued for auditors or insurers.

Off-the-job training: The maritime college course at $750 per employee — $19,500 for 26 staff, modest against a $2,400,000 investment — provides structured, certified learning with up-to-date hospitality technology content and removes staff from the check-in rush. However, the curriculum is generic rather than specific to SBA's exact system, staff leave the floor for days, and the 2.6-day maintenance-resolution KPI could slip while everyone attends.

Decision: SBA should choose on-the-job training for the majority, supplemented by one off-the-job session per front-desk supervisor at the maritime college, with a competency sign-off checklist audited after the first month. This protects the 78% occupancy and the 66% contactless preference during launch, costs far less than $19,500, and is immediately specific to SBA's system and PMS. Full off-the-job training is rejected because pulling 26 staff from live service before the marina apartments open would risk arrival failures precisely when reviews matter most; certified college training can follow later for new hires and refresher compliance once the first guest season has proven the process, and gives SBA an auditable training record for its quality reviews and insurer visits.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to SBA.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of SBA.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of SBA with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and launch risk.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how SBA's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $480,000 ÷ ($52 − $28) = $480,000 ÷ $24 = 20,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 20,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $52 − $28 = $24.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $24.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways SBA's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. SBA's management can compare the 20,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 38,000 units to confirm the marina apartments should be comfortably profitable, with a margin of safety of 18,000 units, supporting the board's decision to commit.
2. Contribution per unit of $24 lets SBA model occupancy-linked discounting to $48 off-peak: contribution falls to $20, and managers can judge whether extra midweek bookings still cover the $480,000 fixed costs.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $480,000 and contribution per unit helps management test whether the $900,000 retained profit portion plus future trading profits can support the share-issue dividend expectations during construction.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($480,000 ÷ 38,000 units + $28 = $40.63 a unit) to benchmark each property, spot maintenance inefficiencies driving the 2.6-day resolution time, and set pricing that protects the $52 average rate.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 20,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $24 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety (18,000 units vs 38,000 output) supports the launch decision; contribution modelling tests off-peak $48 discounting against $480,000 fixed costs; contribution analysis checks dividend capacity after the $1,500,000 share issue; and $40.63 unit cost benchmarks property-level efficiency and maintenance spend across the portfolio.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate SBA's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has SBA's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.25 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.44 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.68 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.98 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $160,000 inventories + $130,000 trade receivables + $60,000 cash = $350,000; 2025 current assets = $130,000 + $165,000 + $115,000 = $410,000. 2024 = $350,000 ÷ $280,000 = 1.25 : 1; 2025 = $410,000 ÷ $285,000 = 1.44 : 1. Excluding inventories: 2024 = ($350,000 − $160,000) ÷ $280,000 = $190,000 ÷ $280,000 = 0.68 : 1; 2025 = ($410,000 − $130,000) ÷ $285,000 = $280,000 ÷ $285,000 = 0.98 : 1.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved. Cover from current assets rose from 1.25 to 1.44, helped by cash almost doubling from $60,000 to $115,000 and inventories falling $30,000 as linen and consumable purchasing became leaner, while current liabilities stayed nearly flat at $285,000. The inventory-excluded measure improved from 0.68 to 0.98 — real progress, though still just below 1.00, thin for a company carrying non-current assets of $10,600,000 and a $2,400,000 marina build. Trade receivables rose from $130,000 to $165,000 (+27%) on long-stay corporate accounts; if those payments slip during construction, cash headroom could vanish quickly. Capital employed rose to $10,900,000, reflecting the investment underway.

Conclusion: SBA's financial position has improved on both measures, but only just crosses into comfortable territory on the stricter measure. SBA should introduce staged corporate billing and a 30-day credit cap before the new apartments open, locking in the improved position rather than spending it during the launch phase of the marina development.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether SBA's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for SBA of introducing contactless check-in across its apartments.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Contactless check-in meets the 66% of guests who prefer it, cutting front-desk queues and redeploying staff into housekeeping consistency — the 57%-rated priority — exactly when 30 new marina apartments add arrival volume. Faster, smoother arrivals lift review scores, support the $52 rack rate during the 5.6% domestic-tourism upturn, and give SBA a marketable tech edge over older properties without longer opening hours or heavier front-desk staffing costs.

Disadvantage: Contactless systems require upfront licence, hardware and cybersecurity spending on top of the $2,400,000 expansion, and guests without smartphones or with poor connectivity may be excluded — a reputational risk while 26 staff are not yet trained on the system. Any outage would inflate the 2.6-day maintenance-complaint trend and undermine the 78% occupancy hard-won this quarter, so SBA must keep staffed desks at peak times and train every front-of-house employee before the full switchover once the first marina guest season has stress-tested the system.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to SBA's guest research, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 8.3% rise in building-material costs will affect SBA. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): SBA financed the marina apartments with a $1,500,000 share issue and $900,000 retained profit, so no loan is attached to the build yet; the direct hit is limited to any bridging or refinancing arranged at 5.0%. Higher rates also cool mortgage-stretched leisure spending, though the 5.6% growth in domestic tourism provides some offset and share funding avoids compounding debt-service costs entirely.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $12.85): With 120 staff heavily weighted to housekeeping and front-desk roles near the minimum, the extra $0.75 per hour is significant. If, for illustration, 70 staff are near the minimum, that is about $108,500 a year — recurring, unavoidable and landing exactly as 30 new apartments add service demand; housekeeping turnover at 22% makes wage dissatisfaction especially corrosive.

Building-material costs (+8.3%): Materials are a major slice of the $2,400,000 marina construction; at an illustrative 50% material share ($1,200,000), an 8.3% rise adds about $100,000 once — painful but one-off, and partly hedged if SBA purchased materials early or renegotiates supplier contracts before winter.

Conclusion: The 6.2% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. Unlike the interest rise, it cannot be dodged through financing structure — SBA's share-and-retained-profit design already neutralises rate risk — and unlike the one-off material overrun, it recurs every year on the largest share of SBA's cost base, rising as the new apartments open. The interest rise is smallest because SBA has no current bank debt, and the material-cost rise is serious but a single-project event. SBA should respond with workforce planning, technology-assisted scheduling, and productivity targets rather than service cuts, protecting the 57% housekeeping-consistency priority.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to SBA.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on SBA's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of SBA with a well-justified judgement that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
